line:
"Brann, keep working that brass ring with whatever oil you have, I'll come back for it." I leave the reliquary seated in the socket, drop down the trapdoor, and take the third step above the doorway just as the crate gives.

As the first pikemen crowd Kit's shield, I cast Faerie Fire at the doorway and the shingle beyond, outlining all of them in light so Kit's attacks have advantage, and call, "Hit the lit ones, Kit, and tell me when you need Healing Word."

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~7:30 AM: his party broke the north door of the Gullspit light. Fight began. Three hired pikemen (statted as Guards) plus Sparrow (statted as a Spy); the Grey Cloak himself stands back on the shingle and has not acted. One pikeman already dead to Kit.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Grey Cloak

You drop down the trapdoor and take the third step above the doorway just as the salt-crate gives. Brann is left muttering at the brass ring above you, and the reliquary stays seated in the lamp's socket. The door bursts inward, and the fight begins before you can speak.

Combat order: the pikemen, then Kit, then you, then Sparrow.

The first pikeman thrusts through the doorway and his spear finds Kit's shoulder for 7. The second drives his spear past his friend's shoulder with a natural 20, and the crit takes Kit down to 3 hit points. Kit grunts and answers with her own natural 20. The longsword takes the first pikeman through the chest and he drops across the threshold. She stands in the doorway with blood down her tabard, shield up, still on her feet.

Two pikemen are left, one in the doorway with his spear still out and one behind him on the shingle. Sparrow stands a few paces back, hands empty and smiling. The tall grey cloak hasn't moved at all, and watches from beside the longboat's prow.

It's your turn, on the third step above the door. You've two 1st-level slots and two Bardic Inspirations (Kit still holds the d6 you gave her). Kit is at 3 hit points. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. Jack of All Trades: Starting at 2nd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any ability check you make that doesn't already include your proficiency bonus.

Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

input.add_to_description: Day 10 ~7:30 AM: fight at the north door. Wren (on stair) cast Faerie Fire; only Guard 2 was lit. Kit holds the doorway with Bardic Inspiration (d6) unused. Grey Cloak stays back on the shingle; Sparrow fires a hand crossbow over the guards.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Gullspit Light

The crate gives with a crack of splintering wood, and you drop to the third step and fling out your hand. Faerie Fire blooms over the doorway and the shingle beyond. The luck is thin, though. Only one of the pikemen fails to dodge, a stocky man in a salt-stained jerkin. Blue light clings to him like paint, and the others and Sparrow slip free of it. You're concentrating on the spell now, and it has cost you a slot. You have one left.

Initiative went Sparrow, you, Kit, then the guards. Sparrow hung back on the shingle and did nothing. Kit stepped into the broken doorway with her shield up and her sword out, and you called the target. She swung at the lit man with advantage and opened his arm to the bone. She still holds your Bardic Inspiration die, unspent. The guards' spear-thrusts rattled off her shield and chain, one spearman so clumsy he nearly speared his own boot. A third guard is jammed behind them and can't reach her. Sparrow lifted a hand crossbow over their shoulders and put a bolt into the doorframe a hand from her ear.

Behind them, a few paces off on the shingle, the tall grey-cloaked figure stands quite still. He hasn't drawn anything, and he's watching the stair, and you.

It's round 2 and your turn. You're on the third step with 17 hit points, one spell slot left, Bardic Inspiration at two uses, and the lamp-staff in your hand. Kit is unhurt. The lit guard is badly hurt and every attack on him has advantage.

What does Wren do?

line:
"A word, Sparrow? Gladly." I keep Ember still and the staff upright, and call to the grey figure, clear enough to carry down the causeway and into the reeds. "Sir, your man says you'd like a word, so take off your hood, let's use your own name, and tell me what you want with a girl and her mother's lamp."

I let that sit a breath, then add, "Because I've been to Thornhallow's register, sir, and Aldous Verrel the younger was baptised a servant's child and buried at three, and his grave doesn't open for a man in a grey cloak." As I finish I swing the lamp-staff up and high, the signal, and cast Faerie Fire at the whole line of them on the road.

input.add_to_description: Day 15 ~2:06 PM: fight begun at the culvert. Wren signalled and cast Faerie Fire (lit Pikeman 1, Pikeman 4, Sparrow; she lost concentration after a crossbow bolt). Kit hit Sparrow for 10. Pell's six guards are running up the causeway. The Grey Cloak stands back and has not drawn a weapon; Wren's challenge about the register was heard by all.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gannet Causeway
Failed. Faerie Fire ends.

You call your challenge down the causeway, loud enough for the reeds to hear: the register, the baptism, the burial at three. The tall man in grey doesn't move, and the hood doesn't turn. Then you swing the lamp-staff high and say the word of Faerie Fire.

Sparrow's line is caught in the light. Pikeman 1, Pikeman 4 and Sparrow fail their saves and stand outlined in cold blue. The other three pikemen shrug it off, and the Grey Cloak, back at the edge of the road, is clear of it. Pell's guards burst from the reeds at the staff and start running the long road toward you.

Kit's crossbow takes Sparrow in the thigh for 10, and he hisses. Pikeman 1's bolt grazes you for 2 (you're at 15 of 17), and that costs you the spell: your concentration save is an 8, so the blue light dies. Pikeman 2 puts a bolt in Kit for 7, and she's at 13 of 20. The other three pikemen close up the road. Sparrow, bleeding, fires at you across the distance and misses by a mile.

It's round 2, your turn. The pikemen are strung out on the narrow road, the nearest about twenty feet off, and the guards are still a long run behind. Sparrow is hurt and the Grey Cloak still stands, hooded, behind his men. You have two 1st-level slots, three Bardic Inspirations, and 15 hit points. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

line:
"A word, Sparrow? Gladly." I keep Ember still and the staff upright, and call to the grey figure, clear enough to carry down the causeway and into the reeds. "Sir, your man says you'd like a word, so take off your hood, let's use your own name, and tell me what you want with a girl and her mother's lamp."

I let that sit a breath, then add, "Because I've been to Thornhallow's register, sir, and Aldous Verrel the younger was baptised a servant's child and buried at three, and his grave doesn't open for a man in a grey cloak." As I finish I swing the lamp-staff up and high, the signal, and cast Faerie Fire at the whole line of them on the road.

You speak plainly, loud enough to carry down the causeway and into the reeds: take off the hood, use your own name, and know that Aldous Verrel the younger was a servant's child, baptised and buried at three, and that his grave doesn't open for a man in a grey cloak.

The tall figure doesn't answer. He doesn't move. That silence is the answer, and Sparrow's smile thins.

Sparrow doesn't wait for your staff to fall. He won initiative, and his hand crossbow is up before you finish the last word. The bolt takes you in the ribs for 8, so you're at 9 of 17. Kit, at the wheel, snaps a bolt back at him for 7, and he's hurt. Two pikemen charge into her shield and both swings glance off it.

Then your turn. You swing the lamp-staff high, the signal, and cast Faerie Fire at the whole crowded line on the road (one slot spent, two left). Sparrow fails his save with a 6. Bandits 1, 3 and 5 fail theirs too (a 7, a natural 1, and a 9). Bandits 2 and 4 make theirs and stay in shadow. Four of them now stand outlined in blue light, and anything that attacks them has advantage. You are concentrating on the spell and have been hit once since, but the save isn't needed yet.

The grey-cloaked man still hasn't moved, still hooded, still unlit, ten paces behind his men with his left hand resting at his belt and the green ring sparking in the sun. In the reeds behind you, you hear Pell's low shout and the rustle of eight boots coming out of the mud toward both ends of the culvert. They're a round away.

Corvin sits very still on the wagon bench, and the tide is running out on both sides. It is round 2 next, and Sparrow acts first. What does Wren do with the rest of her turn?
You have 9 of 17 hit points, two 1st-level slots, three Bardic Inspirations, and your bonus action still open.
